opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I wouldn't say I was fully confident at the beginning. It was more of a bet, but one with some reasoning behind it.

The robot was built cheaply. The joints had backlash, the chopsticks flexed, and the calibration was never perfect. If you tried to control it the classical way, by building an accurate kinematic model and computing exactly where the tips should go, the errors would pile up. You'd be off by millimeters, and with chopsticks, millimeters decide whether you pick up the object or knock it away.

What gave me hope was watching people. Humans aren't precise machines either. Our muscles are noisy, our perception is imperfect, and no one computes the exact geometry of a pair of chopsticks before eating. Yet we can pick up a peanut. We do it with feedback and a lot of practice. We learn how our own imperfect bodies behave, and we correct as we go.

So the question became: what if the robot doesn't need to be accurate in absolute terms, but only needs to be consistent enough that its mistakes can be learned? If the error is systematic, like a joint that always sags a little in a certain pose, then data captures it. A learned policy can absorb that error without anyone modeling it explicitly. Closing the loop with vision helps too. The robot doesn't have to get it right open-loop. It just needs to see that it's off and nudge itself back.

There was also a practical side. We could collect demonstrations relatively cheaply, so the data-driven route was something we could actually iterate on, instead of spending months on a perfect model that would break the moment a screw loosened.

And I think there was a philosophical motivation. If we only make robots work by making the hardware extremely precise, robots stay expensive and fragile. If learning can compensate for imperfect hardware, that opens the door to cheap robots that can still do delicate things. The chopsticks were a nice stress test for that idea: a deliberately humble, imprecise tool performing a task that demands finesse.

So it wasn't certainty. It was a belief that precision can come from the loop, meaning data, feedback, and correction, rather than only from the mechanism. The experiments ended up supporting that more than I expected.

r001.rationale: The response argues that feedback and learning could compensate for mechanical errors, but it does not present successful human teleoperation of the robot or say that this demonstrated its ability to pick up a small ball.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started with a bit of a bet against myself. The robot we built was deliberately cheap. The chopsticks were held by a simple gripper, there was compliance and slop in the joints, and if you measured where the tip actually landed versus where the kinematics said it should be, the error was on the order of millimeters. For picking up a grain of rice or a slippery piece of tofu, that's a lot.

The traditional reaction is to engineer the error away. Stiffer linkages, better encoders, careful calibration. But I had spent enough time watching people use chopsticks to notice that humans are also mechanically terrible. Our hands shake, our grip shifts, the chopsticks slide in our fingers. We never compute where the tip is. We look, we feel the contact, and we correct. The precision comes from the feedback loop, not from the hardware.

So the question became whether a learned controller could close that same loop. And there were two things that made me confident rather than just hopeful. The first was that the errors in our robot were systematic rather than random. The arm sagged the same way every time, the chopsticks slipped in predictable directions. Anything systematic is learnable. If you collect enough demonstrations and the model sees the camera image together with the outcome, it can absorb that bias implicitly. It doesn't need to know the arm is bent, it just learns that this image means move a little more to the left.

The second was that we had cameras close to the task. Once you put a wrist camera right above the chopstick tips, the model doesn't have to trust the kinematics at all. It can see the gap between the tips and the object directly. That turns a hard global precision problem into a local servoing problem, and local servoing is very forgiving of a bad robot.

I'll admit there was also an element of stubbornness. We had already tried calibrating it properly, and every time we touched the chopsticks or swapped a gripper pad the calibration went stale. Data-driven methods were the only approach that didn't fall apart when the hardware changed. And when the first policy picked up a slippery bean on a robot I knew was inaccurate, that was the moment I stopped thinking of hardware precision as the bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response says human chopstick use inspired feedback control and describes a policy picking up a slippery bean, but it does not present successful human teleoperation of the robot or a small ball as evidence.

astra-6.text: The intuition was that mechanical inaccuracy doesn’t necessarily mean the robot is impossible to control. If the errors are consistent enough, a data-driven method can learn how the robot actually behaves, rather than relying on an idealized model. With feedback, it can then correct the remaining error. So the question was whether we could learn that relationship well enough to get precise behavior out of imperfect hardware.

r001.rationale: The response says data-driven learning and feedback could compensate for consistent mechanical errors, but it does not mention successful human teleoperation or picking up a small ball as evidence.

sol-6.1.text: The key intuition was that mechanical inaccuracy doesn’t necessarily mean the errors are unpredictable. If the robot behaves consistently enough, we can collect data and learn the relationship between the commands we send and what the chopsticks actually do. Then we can use feedback to correct the remaining error. So my confidence wasn’t that data would somehow fix the mechanics—it was that we could learn to compensate for their imperfections well enough to achieve precise manipulation.
